video_title: Stripe’s John Collison: AI Agents Will Rewire the Internet
gist: Stripe co-founder John Collison (on stage with Molly O'Shea at a Browserbase event) argues agentic commerce and computer use will rewire online buying and aggregation, explains Stripe's AI-era acquisitions (Metronome, Bridge, Privy, OpenRouter) as bets on usage-based billing, crypto and multi-model routing, and reports record new-firm creation alongside a warning of rising AI-driven breaches. Stripe processed $1.9T in 2025, up 34%.

insights.claim: John Collison expects personal AI agents to do a huge amount of consumer commerce on people's behalf, since filling out web forms adds no value for anyone and agents with stateful context (shipping address, payment details) can execute tasks instead.
insights.speaker: John Collison
insights.so_what: Checkout, payments and merchant integration layers must be rebuilt for agent-initiated transactions.
insights.quote: filling out a web form is not a value ad activity for anyone

insights.claim: Collison argues AI-driven product discovery is becoming the new point of aggregation for commerce, which will force existing aggregators to answer hard questions.
insights.speaker: John Collison
insights.so_what: Incumbent marketplaces and search/ads aggregators face disintermediation risk from AI shopping assistants.
insights.quote: AI discovery is the new point of aggregation for commerce

insights.claim: Collison says AI-powered product research often surfaces niche brands, making agentic commerce a good story for long-tail merchants with genuinely well-reviewed products.
insights.speaker: John Collison
insights.so_what: Favors quality DTC/niche brands and tools that make products discoverable to AI agents.
insights.quote: it often actually surfaces niche brands or businesses you haven't heard of

insights.claim: Collison predicts AI commerce will cause a turnover of top merchants, analogous to how Facebook/Instagram ad targeting birthed natively-adapted winners like Wish.com, Teespring, Temu and Shein that out-acquired big box retailers.
insights.speaker: John Collison
insights.so_what: Expect a new generation of AI-native merchants to take share; legacy retailers slow to adapt are at risk.
insights.quote: you probably have a bit of a turning over of the top businesses

insights.claim: Collison frames agentic commerce as first-order more convenient buying and second-order a reshaping of the product and merchant landscape favoring those who adopt it most successfully, flowing all the way down to product creation.
insights.speaker: John Collison
insights.so_what: Second-order effects (who wins as merchant) matter more than the convenience layer for investors.

insights.claim: Collison flags bot detection as an under-asked question: sites block bots today, but traffic is increasingly all bots, so a new mechanism is needed to distinguish good bots (agents) from bad bots.
insights.speaker: John Collison
insights.so_what: Opportunity for agent identity/verification and good-bot authentication infrastructure.

insights.claim: Collison calls computer use the ultimate backwards-compatibility layer for the real world, letting agents operate legacy systems like the DMV without waiting years for them to add an MCP server.
insights.speaker: John Collison
insights.so_what: Computer-use/browser infrastructure (e.g., Browserbase) may capture value regardless of API/MCP adoption pace.
insights.quote: computer use is the ultimate backwards compatibility layer for the real world

insights.claim: Collison believes good computer use will come to be viewed as the next discrete hop in AI progress, after transformers, LLMs and RL, and will drive the next wave of AI applications.
insights.speaker: John Collison
insights.so_what: Positions computer-use capability as a major platform shift worth tracking for application-layer bets.
insights.quote: good computer use is like will come to be viewed as one of these next hops

insights.claim: Collison says giving personal agents a meaningful amount of compute, plus mature computer use, is what makes personal agents start to work, and recommends trying assistants like Instinct, Grok bot or Meta's Muse to sense what's coming.
insights.speaker: John Collison
insights.so_what: Compute per agent and computer-use maturity are the gating factors for consumer agent adoption.

insights.claim: Collison says Browserbase is well on its way to becoming a huge Stripe customer, and Stripe tracks fast-growing companies on its platform, which are invariably in or around AI.
insights.speaker: John Collison
insights.so_what: Signals strong revenue traction at Browserbase per Stripe's view of its payment volume.
insights.quote: browser base is well on its way to becoming a huge uh stripe company

insights.claim: Stripe processed $1.9 trillion in payment volume in 2025, up 34%, per the host's introduction, which Collison echoes when describing reaching 1.9 trillion.
insights.speaker: Molly O'Shea
insights.so_what: 34% growth at ~$1.9T scale signals accelerating online GDP and Stripe share gains.
insights.quote: Stripe processed $1.9 trillion dollar in 2025, up 34%

insights.claim: Collison says no one integrates the Stripe API by hand anymore; coding agents do it, and AI ergonomics differ from developer ergonomics (e.g., agents easily integrate the wrong API version), forcing Stripe to change what it's good at.
insights.speaker: John Collison
insights.so_what: Developer-experience moats are being reset; API vendors must optimize for agent integrators.
insights.quote: No one actually really integrates the Stripe API by hand anymore.

insights.claim: Collison explains Stripe acquired Bridge and Privy to inject crypto-nativity into its culture that would be hard to build internally quickly.
insights.speaker: John Collison
insights.so_what: Stripe is committed to crypto/stablecoin rails via acqui-culture, not just product.

insights.claim: Collison says Stripe bought Metronome because AI inference costs mean almost every AI product now needs usage-based billing or overages, as with ChatGPT and Claude credit purchases.
insights.speaker: John Collison
insights.so_what: Usage-based billing infrastructure is becoming mandatory across software as inference costs pass through.
insights.quote: everyone needs to have usage based billing these days

insights.claim: Collison says Stripe acquired OpenRouter because an increasing fraction of business spend goes to AI inference and businesses will use multiple models simultaneously, routing by workload or user lifetime value (frontier model for high-value users, cheaper models for low-value).
insights.speaker: John Collison
insights.so_what: Bet against single-model winner-take-all; model routing marketplaces become a payments-adjacent control point.
insights.quote: to believe in open router you have to believe that more than one model will be used inside a business

insights.claim: Collison's build-vs-buy rule: Stripe builds things close to its core, but buys for new muscles in fast-evolving markets like token routing, since an internal effort would be out of date by completion; OpenRouter's market is totally different from 12 months ago.
insights.speaker: John Collison
insights.so_what: Expect Stripe to keep acquiring in fast-moving AI infra categories adjacent to payments.
insights.quote: by the time you build your internal effort it'll be a little bit out of date

insights.claim: Collison declines to give the exact share of Stripe volume from AI but says it is 'a lot', noting AI vs non-AI segmentation is hard since incumbents like Meta, which runs on Stripe, are becoming AI companies.
insights.speaker: John Collison
insights.so_what: AI is a material and growing driver of Stripe volume, though undisclosed.
insights.quote: I won't say the exact fraction, but a lot

insights.claim: Stripe tongue-in-cheek dates the singularity epoch to January 1, 2026, following the late-2025 'holy crap moment' in coding models, with 2026 being the year recursive self-improvement is felt (including labs using AI to speed model development and 'math wars').
insights.speaker: John Collison
insights.so_what: Signals top-tier operators view AI takeoff as underway now, supporting aggressive AI investment pacing.

insights.claim: Collison reports Stripe is seeing the highest rate of new firm creation in recent memory, attributing it to cheaper intelligence on tap making companies easier to start and grow.
insights.speaker: John Collison
insights.so_what: Leading indicator for SMB/startup formation and demand for business-infrastructure tooling.
insights.quote: We're seeing the highest rate of um of new firm creation that we've seen in recent memory on Stripe

insights.claim: Collison says internal Stripe AI tools connected to internal data (with privacy and access-control guardrails) changed workflows: sales teams build their own pitch apps and a legal team member built an agent to ingest new global regulation, showing personalized software finally arriving.
insights.speaker: John Collison
insights.so_what: Enterprise value accrues to permissioned internal-data AI layers; personalized/vibe-coded software is going mainstream.
insights.quote: finally the barrier to entry has gotten low enough that we are now seeing a huge amount of personalized software

insights.claim: Collison predicts more breaches over the next five years than the past five, as new models' advanced cyber capabilities improve attackers quickly and many organizations are too slow to adopt defenses.
insights.speaker: John Collison
insights.so_what: Tailwind for cybersecurity spending; elevated breach risk for slow-moving legacy enterprises.
insights.quote: over the next five years you're going to see more breaches than you did over the past five years

insights.claim: Collison argues startups are disproportionately well positioned on AI-era cyber because they can adopt latest models and have smaller homogeneous stacks, versus acquisition-built 50-year-old stacks running unsupported Windows.
insights.speaker: John Collison
insights.so_what: Legacy incumbents with sprawling tech stacks carry hidden cyber liability.

insights.claim: Collison says Stripe never had a breakout moment; it compounded by growing every year and reached $1.9 trillion through persistence, rarely starting products that seemed like the company's future at the time.
insights.speaker: John Collison
insights.so_what: Durable compounding and small-bet product expansion beat hype cycles in infrastructure businesses.
insights.quote: Stripe never had a South by Southwest breakout moment

insights.claim: Collison cites Nvidia as a stick-with-it story, making GPUs since the 1990s and adding CUDA, through many periods when it was much less hot than today.
insights.speaker: John Collison
insights.so_what: Reinforces patience thesis for long-horizon infrastructure holdings.
